lessons.title: Load average and uptime
lessons.goal:
Learn what the three load average numbers mean, how to compare them with the number of CPUs, and why a high load does not always mean a busy CPU.

Why it matters: load average is the most quoted and most misread number in Linux. Reading it correctly is the first step of every performance investigation.

setup.note: Steps start a few busy loops (`sh -c 'while :; do :; done'`) and stop them again. This machine has 1 CPU, which makes load easy to read.

steps.title: Where to read it
steps.text: `uptime` prints the time since boot, the number of users and the **load averages** for the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes. The same numbers are the first three fields of `/proc/loadavg`; the fourth is `running/total` tasks and the fifth the last PID.

run.cmd: cat /proc/loadavg | awk '{print "1 min:", $1, " 5 min:", $2, " 15 min:", $3, " running/total:", $4}'

steps.title: What is being averaged
steps.text: Every few seconds the kernel counts the tasks that are **runnable** (running or waiting for a CPU, state `R`) **plus** those in **uninterruptible sleep** (`D`, usually waiting for disk or NFS), and keeps three exponentially damped averages of that count. So load measures **demand** for CPU *and* for I/O, not CPU use.

run.cmd: ps -eo stat | grep -c '^D' | awk '{print $1, "task(s) in D state now"}'

steps.title: Make load by hand
steps.text: We start three busy loops for 30 seconds. On one CPU, one is running and two are waiting. The load rises toward 3, but slowly, because it is a damped average.

run.cmd: before=$(cut -d' ' -f1 /proc/loadavg); pids=""; for i in 1 2 3; do sh -c 'while :; do :; done' & pids="$pids $!"; done; sleep 30; after=$(cut -d' ' -f1 /proc/loadavg); echo "1-minute load before: $before, after 30 s: $after"; grep procs_running /proc/stat

steps.after: `procs_running` counted our three loops (plus the command reading it). The 1-minute value had moved up but not yet to 3: a 1-minute average needs about 3 minutes to settle.

steps.title: Reading the numbers
steps.text:
Compare the load with the number of CPUs:

- load **below** the CPU count: spare capacity.
- load **at** the CPU count: fully busy but not waiting.
- load **above** it: tasks are queuing.

The three averages show the trend: `1 > 5 > 15` means it is getting busier, `1 < 5 < 15` means it is calming down. A load of 40 with idle CPUs means many tasks in `D` state (I/O or NFS stalls): look at `ps -eo stat,wchan` (lab: "high load with idle CPU").

run.cmd: ps -eo stat,comm | awk '$1 ~ /^R/ {r++} $1 ~ /^D/ {d++} END {print "runnable:", r+0, " uninterruptible:", d+0}'

steps.under: The kernel updates the averages every 5 seconds with `load = load * e + n * (1 - e)`, where `n` is the current count and `e` is `exp(-5/60)` for the 1-minute average (`exp(-5/300)` and `exp(-5/900)` for the others). That is why changes show up slowly. Other systems (Solaris, BSD) count only CPU demand; Linux's inclusion of `D` state is deliberate: it measures *tasks wanting resources*.

quiz.q: What does a Linux load average of 4.0 on a 4-CPU machine mean?
options: On average four tasks wanted a CPU (or waited for I/O): the CPUs are just fully used
quiz.explain: Load equal to the CPU count is full use without queuing.

quiz.q: Which states count toward Linux load?
Load average is 30, CPU is 95% idle. What is the most likely cause?
options: Many tasks stuck in D state waiting for I/O
quiz.explain: Blocked tasks count but use no CPU.

check.scenario: A monitoring alert says "load 12 on an 8-CPU database server", but `top` shows 30% CPU. What are your next two commands and what do you look for?
check.answer: `vmstat 1 5` (columns `r` run queue, `b` blocked, `wa` I/O wait, `si/so` swap) and `ps -eo pid,stat,wchan:30,comm | awk '$2 ~ /^D/'` to list tasks in D state and where they wait. A high `b`/`wa` with D-state tasks points to storage (see `iostat -x`) or NFS; a high `r` with low idle points to real CPU saturation.

lessons.title: The USE method: utilization, saturation, errors
lessons.goal:
Apply a simple checklist to every resource (CPU, memory, disk, network): how **utilised** is it, is work **queueing** (saturation), and are there **errors**.

Why it matters: instead of running random tools, USE gives a fixed order of questions that finds most bottlenecks quickly, and tells you when a resource is fine and you can stop looking at it.

setup.note: Steps start a few busy loops (`sh -c 'while :; do :; done'`) and stop them again. This machine has 1 CPU, which makes load easy to read.

steps.title: The method
steps.text:
For each resource ask three questions: **U**tilization (how busy: percent of time or capacity used), **S**aturation (is there extra work waiting: a queue, swapping), **E**rrors (counters of failures). Check errors first (they are cheap and decisive), then saturation, then utilization.

| Resource | Utilization | Saturation | Errors |
|---|---|---|---|
| CPU | `mpstat`: %usr+%sys | run queue `vmstat r` > CPUs | machine check, `dmesg` |
| Memory | `free`: used/available | swapping `si/so`, OOM kills | `dmesg` OOM, failed allocations |
| Disk | `iostat %util` | `aqu-sz`, `await` | `dmesg` I/O errors, SMART |
| Network | `sar -n DEV` vs link speed | drops, retransmits | `ip -s link` errors |

steps.title: CPU: utilization and saturation
steps.text: `vmstat 1 3` prints one line per second. `r` is the number of runnable tasks (saturation if above the CPU count); `us`, `sy`, `id`, `wa`, `st` are the CPU shares (utilization). The first line is the average since boot; ignore it for current state.

run.cmd: vmstat 1 3 | awk 'NR==2 {print "r b | us sy id wa st"} NR>2 {print $1, $2, "|", $13, $14, $15, $16, $17}'

steps.title: Memory
steps.text: Utilization is **used** and **available** in `free`. Saturation is swapping: `si`/`so` in `vmstat` (pages swapped in and out per second). Errors are OOM kills in the kernel log.

run.cmd: free -m | awk 'NR==1 {print "      total used free available"} NR==2 {print "Mem:  ", $2, $3, $4, $7}'
vmstat 1 2 | tail -n 1 | awk '{print "swap in/out per s:", $7, $8}'
sudo dmesg | grep -ci 'out of memory' | awk '{print $1, "OOM message(s) in the kernel log"}'
run.output: 9 OOM message(s) in the kernel log

steps.title: Disk
steps.text: `iostat -x` gives `%util` (utilization), `aqu-sz` and `await` (saturation and latency) per device. Errors show in `dmesg` and SMART.

run.cmd: iostat -dx 1 2 sda | awk '/^Device/ {for (i=1;i<=NF;i++) c[$i]=i} $1=="sda" {u=$c["%util"]; q=$c["aqu-sz"]; a=$c["w_await"]} END {print "sda: %util", u, " aqu-sz", q, " w_await ms", a}'
sudo dmesg | grep -ciE 'I/O error.*(sd[a-z]|nvme)' | awk '{print $1, "I/O error message(s) for physical disks"}'
run.output: 0 I/O error message(s) for physical disks

steps.title: Network
steps.text: `ip -s link` shows packet and byte counters plus **errors** and **drops** per interface. On loopback there should be none. For real NICs compare throughput with the link speed.

run.cmd: ip -s link show lo | awk 'NR==3 {h=$0} NR==4 {print "RX:", "packets", $2, "errors", $3, "dropped", $4}'
sar -n DEV 1 1 | grep -E 'Average.*[[:space:]]lo[[:space:]]' | awk '{print "lo rx kB/s:", $5, "tx kB/s:", $6}'

steps.under: USE comes from Brendan Gregg's performance work. Its strength is **completeness**: you walk through every resource instead of guessing. Its limit: it finds resource bottlenecks, not software ones (lock contention, slow queries). For those use latency-oriented methods (RED for services: Rate, Errors, Duration) and profilers.

quiz.q: What do the letters in USE stand for?
Which `vmstat` column indicates CPU saturation when higher than the CPU count?

quiz.explain: Work waiting for memory means paging or killing.

options: They are cheap to check and decisive when present
Required by the method order only
quiz.explain: A failing disk explains everything quickly.

check.scenario: A web server is slow. Walk through USE for the four resources in a sentence each, naming the command.
check.answer: CPU: `mpstat -P ALL 1` and `vmstat r` (busy or queueing?). Memory: `free -m` and `vmstat si so` plus `dmesg | grep -i oom`. Disk: `iostat -x 1` (`%util`, `await`, `aqu-sz`) and `dmesg` for I/O errors. Network: `sar -n DEV 1` against link speed, `ip -s link` and `ss -s`/`nstat` for drops and retransmits. The first resource with high utilization **and** saturation (or any errors) is the lead.

interview.a: An exponentially damped average (1, 5, 15 minutes) of the number of tasks that are runnable or in uninterruptible sleep. See [the lesson](#/lesson/41/load-average).
Only relative to the number of CPUs and to what is queueing. 10 on 16 CPUs is fine; 10 on 2 CPUs means queueing. And D-state tasks raise it without using CPU.
For every resource check Utilization, Saturation and Errors, errors first. See [the lesson](#/lesson/41/use-method).

interview.q: High load, idle CPU: what is it?
interview.a: Many tasks in D state (disk or NFS waits). Find them with `ps -eo stat,wchan` and check `iostat -x` and NFS mounts.

interview.q: Why does the 1-minute load average lag?
interview.a: It is a damped average updated every 5 seconds; a change takes minutes to be fully reflected.
USE is for resources (hosts, disks, links); RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) is for request-driven services. Use both: services on top of resources.

glossary.def: The damped average of runnable plus uninterruptible tasks over 1, 5 and 15 minutes.
The tasks waiting for a CPU.
A checklist: utilization, saturation and errors for every resource.
Extra work waiting because a resource is fully used (queues, swapping).
CPU idle time during which tasks waited for I/O.

commands.desc: System-wide CPU, memory, swap and I/O each second.
Interface counters including errors and drops.
